title: Arrested at his green card interview over a notice sent to the wrong address, a Canadian dentist is freed by a federal judge
dek: Judge Michael Davis ruled ICE's arrest of William Lizardo violated the Fourth and Fifth Amendments, faulting the government for conceding its own mistake while fighting to keep him locked up.
body:
A federal judge in Minnesota ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Sunday to release William Virgil Lizardo, a 32-year-old Canadian dentist who was arrested by ICE agents at the end of his own green card interview. U.S. District Judge Michael J. Davis found that the arrest and the nine days of detention that followed violated both the Fourth and Fifth Amendments, and that there was an “obvious” risk Lizardo had been wrongly deprived of his liberty [1].

The case turned on a piece of mail. Davis found that the government ordered Lizardo deported after he missed a hearing he was never properly told about, because the notice went to an address the government's own files showed he had left. Then, when he showed up in person to pursue his green card, ICE used that removal order to arrest him [1][3]. Davis called the facts of the case “appalling” [1].

## Who Lizardo is

Lizardo is a Canadian citizen from Mississauga, Ontario. He came to the United States in 2019 on an F-1 student visa to attend the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry, and graduated in 2023 [1]. He married Lauren, a U.S. citizen and dental-school classmate, and the couple had a daughter in spring 2025 [1]. The family lives in Victoria, Minnesota, a suburb southwest of the Twin Cities [2].

After graduating, he worked in areas the federal government designates as short of dental care. When his work authorization was revoked, he began volunteering at a low-cost dental clinic in Burnsville [1][2]. Trade publication Oral Health Group, which covers the Canadian dental profession, followed the case from his arrest to his release [4][5].

## How a green card case became a deportation order

The family took the standard route to permanent residence for the spouse of a U.S. citizen. Lauren Lizardo filed a petition for her husband in September 2023, and it was approved in January 2025. He also applied to adjust his status to permanent resident [1].

In January 2026, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services denied that application. According to Newsweek, the reason was a missing document: a certified court record from Ontario for a 2012 charge that was withdrawn after Lizardo completed a diversion program. He appealed, and that appeal was still pending at the time of this weekend's ruling [1].

In February, the government issued a Notice to Appear, the document that starts deportation proceedings, setting a hearing for March 26. It was mailed to an address in Virginia that the family says they had moved out of more than two years earlier [2][3]. Newsweek reports the court found that address conflicted with newer address information USCIS had on file [1]. Lizardo never received it. When he did not appear on March 26, an immigration judge ordered him removed in absentia, the term for a deportation order issued when someone misses their hearing [1].

His wife told CBS Minnesota that the couple checked their online immigration case portal every day, and that other USCIS mail had been reaching them at their current address [2]. Davis later found that the agency's own records showed Lizardo no longer lived at the Virginia address [1][3].

## The arrest

On Friday, October 23, Lizardo went to his green card interview in the Twin Cities. Reports differ on whether the appointment was in St. Paul or downtown Minneapolis [1][2]. His lawyer at the time, David Whalen, told CBS Minnesota that the officer conducting the interview left the room and came back with two ICE agents, who took Lizardo into custody [2]. He was held at the Sherburne County Jail, which houses ICE detainees under a contract with the federal government [1][3].

ICE's position, as stated to CBS that week, was straightforward: a records check showed Lizardo had a final order of removal, and an application for immigration relief, pending or new, does not stop ICE from enforcing such an order. The agency called him an illegal alien from Canada who had overstayed his lawful entry, and said those who break the law will face consequences. It did not respond to the claim that the hearing notice went to the wrong address [2]. Whalen called Lizardo probably the best candidate he had ever represented and said the government had made a mistake [2].

Arrests at marriage-based green card interviews have drawn legal challenges elsewhere this year. A federal judge in Maryland, George Hazel, issued an injunction in February limiting arrests at marriage interviews there, and an arrest at a Salt Lake City green card interview drew attention in December 2025 [9][11].

## The case unravels in immigration court

Lizardo's lawyers moved quickly. On October 25, two days after the arrest, he asked the immigration court to reopen his case and rescind the removal order because he had never been notified of the hearing. On October 28, the court granted the motion [1]. That meant the deportation order ICE had relied on for the arrest no longer existed.

The government did not release him. According to Newsweek, government lawyers instead asked the federal court to dismiss his habeas petition, arguing that with the case reopened he was now being held under a different provision of immigration law [1]. Ahmad, Lizardo's lawyer, told Newsweek that the government sought dismissal without first getting the court's permission and pressed Lizardo to accept voluntary departure to Canada [1].

## What the judge decided

Davis granted the habeas petition on Sunday, November 1 [1][3]. His reasoning, as described in coverage of the order, ran along two constitutional lines.

On the Fourth Amendment, which bars unreasonable seizures, Davis found that USCIS lacked probable cause to believe Lizardo was in the country unlawfully, because its own files showed the hearing notice had gone to an outdated address. An arrest built on that removal order, in his view, was not a lawful seizure [3].

On the Fifth Amendment's due process guarantee, Davis found nothing to justify continued detention: no new warrant, no new custody determination and no evidence that Lizardo was a flight risk. He pointed to Lizardo's record of attending every hearing he knew about, keeping USCIS informed of his address, his lack of any U.S. criminal record, his wife and daughter, his volunteer dental work and more than a dozen letters of support. It strained credulity, the judge wrote, to think such a person would flee [3].

Davis's sharpest words were aimed at the government's litigation posture. He described as hubris, and as galling though not surprising, the government's admission that USCIS had made a big mistake while offering no relief for it [1][12].

The order required Lizardo's release on his own recognizance by 6 p.m. Sunday [1][12], with his belongings returned. It bars the government from re-detaining him, transferring him or removing him from the country without the court's permission. If the government later wants to detain him, it must cite its legal authority, show that circumstances have materially changed, and prove by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions could ensure he shows up for proceedings and poses no danger [1].

The order does not give Lizardo a green card, and it does not decide his reopened immigration case [1].

## Release, and what comes next

Lizardo walked out of the Sherburne County Jail shortly before 9 p.m. Sunday, hours past the deadline, according to his lawyer at the ruling stage, Hassan Ahmad. Ahmad said jail staff told him they had to wait for word from ICE, and that an emergency 9:30 p.m. Zoom hearing was called off once Lizardo was out [1].

Ahmad was blunt. He said the government knew it had made a serious mistake and kept fighting to hold his client anyway, and he disputed ICE's claim that Lizardo had overstayed. The next step, he said, is getting the green card approved [1][3]. That still depends on the pending appeal of the USCIS denial and on the reopened case in immigration court [1].

After the ruling, ICE declined to comment and referred questions to the Department of Homeland Security. Newsweek reported that DHS had not responded to its request for comment, and no outlet had reported an appeal as of Monday [1][3].

## The bigger picture in Minnesota

The case lands in a federal district that has become one of the busiest battlegrounds over immigration detention. After the administration's enforcement surge in Minnesota, known as Operation Metro Surge, began in December 2025, the state's federal courts received more than 1,000 habeas petitions by mid-February 2026, compared with 73 in the previous twelve months, according to the Minnesota Reformer. Judges appointed by presidents of both parties have ordered releases or bond hearings in many of them [6].

The administration's view is that it is enforcing the law as written. It treats many people without settled status as applicants for admission who are subject to mandatory detention, and it says its priority is removing dangerous offenders. A federal appeals court, the Fifth Circuit, has upheld that mandatory-detention reading [6]. DHS has accused what it calls activist judges of trying to block the president's deportation agenda, and has said arrests in Minnesota will continue [7]. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in October that the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history [4].

The friction between the courts and ICE in Minnesota has not eased. Last week another Minnesota federal judge, Jeffrey Bryan, threatened ICE with sanctions after it re-arrested an asylum seeker the court had ordered released; DHS responded that ICE complies with lawful court orders and that a release does not shield anyone from future enforcement [8].

Davis, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton in 1993, served as the district's chief judge from 2008 to 2015 and has been on senior status since 2015 [10]. His order in Lizardo's case is narrow: it frees one man and limits what the government can do to him next. But it puts a federal judge's findings on the record that, in this case, the error began with the government's own paperwork.
